title: Errors, warnings and status notes still print millimeters in inch documents
body:
Found while auditing every user-visible string that carries a unit suffix.

**What happens:** the mm/inch choice is a document-level lens (`app::units`,
set from the Stock page), applied at the parameter widgets, the parameter
tables and the post. It is *not* applied to the strings the app says at
itself: refusals, machine-limit warnings, simulation verdicts and status
notices are built with `format!("… {x:.3} mm")` over the raw internal
millimeter value. In an inch document every one of those sentences reads in
millimeters, with the internal number, so it cannot be read against the inch
values the user typed a screen earlier.

**Confirmed on `main` b6516886**, by reading the string builders:

- app refusal - `commands/set_stock.rs:47`: "stock dimensions exceed
  2000 mm", against a box the user stated in inches;
- machine limits - `machine/mod.rs:229,235,331`: "move 12 feeds 3000
  mm/min, X tops out at {ceiling}", a stated feed and a stated ceiling
  shown in a unit the document does not use;
- ui status and labels - `state.rs:2681` ("suggestion applied - 3180 rpm,
  480 mm/min"), `egui_app/feeds_page.rs:104` ("fz 0.050 mm"),
  `egui_app/setup_stock_pick.rs:69,72` (incoming-box range and `mm3`
  volume), `actions.rs:289,298` ("removed 12.500 mm3" beside a table that
  shows inches), `app/src/posting_sim.rs:60` ("worst 0.25 mm");
- generator refusals and notes - `operation/circle_fit.rs:67`,
  `operation/cross_stock.rs:282,301`, `operation/drill_reach.rs:71,169,194`,
  `operation/probe.rs:183`, `tool_body.rs:87,150`,
  `commands/cutting_data.rs:80`, `cutting.rs:199`.

The strings fall into two tiers, and they fix differently:

1. **Transient** - a status line, a refusal, a gate note, read once. These
   lens at the point they are built: `units::of(&world)` where the world is
   at hand, the pure `units::len/feed/area` formatters otherwise - they
   already exist and already do this job at the table edges.
   `geometry::units` has no volume formatter, so the `mm3` strings need one
   added there.
2. **Persisted into the document** - an op note, `path.notes`, the setup
   sheet, and from there the NC program header: `stock_sim.rs:523`,
   `commands/sync_stock.rs:181,183`, `operation/carried_stock.rs:215`. A
   lensed string frozen at generation time restates itself wrongly, because
   the unit is a lens that can flip after the generation. These want the
   structured-note pattern the sim warnings already use -
   `sim::verify::Warning` carries a number and the ui renders it through the
   lens (`sim_readout`) - so they are their own change.

Not reached by either: refusals whose `Display` lives in a crate with no
world (`tools/src/spun.rs:79,90`, `tools/src/holder_profile.rs:94`,
`tools/src/lathe_holder.rs:95-97`, `tools/src/lathe_insert_zone.rs:48`,
`motion/src/descent.rs:263`, `motion/src/probing.rs:149`) - lensing those
means plumbing `Unit` into the formatter itself.

**Adjacent, and a worse bug than this one, not part of it:** an inch machine
def's stated numbers are read as millimeters.
`assets/machines/tormach-pcnc440.mch` declares `"units": { "length": "inch" }`
with Z travel `-10.0..10.0`, and `machine::check_ops` compares program
coordinates, which are always millimeters, straight against those bands - a
mounted 440 refuses any move past 10 mm. Nothing converts a machine def's
numbers on read; there is no `MM_PER_INCH` in the machine reader.

**Done means:** the tier-1 strings render through the lens, pinned at app
and ui level, and `geometry::units` gains the volume formatter. The tier-2
notes stay frozen until the structured-note change.

Filed by an agent: `source:agent`, `P2`, `area:ui` - gh will not let a
non-member add labels, so they need applying by a member.

title: Probe posts: report the measured deviation on the control (e.g. PathPilot DEBUG) before writing the offset

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Asked by the contributor after #521's hands-on probe run on a real Tormach 770MX, 2026-11-09: "did the probe report any issues or changes from expected? If so, where/how?"

**Today:** a probing program is silent when it succeeds. It stores the trip point (`#100..`), computes the error (`#190=[#102-0]`), stops with a message only when the error is out of tolerance (`(MSG, PROBE Z OUT OF TOLERANCE)` + `M2`), and otherwise rewrites the work offset with `G10 L20` without a word.
- **On the 770MX:** G54 Z moved from -8.3252 to -8.3259 (the top read 0.0007 in low). The offset table was the only trace, and the operator could not tell from the screen what the probe measured or what it changed.

**Expected:** before the offset write, the post reports the measured deviation per probed axis on the control's operator-message channel. The program does not stop for it.
- **Tormach/LinuxCNC:** `(DEBUG, PROBE Z ERROR #190)`. PathPilot shows DEBUG lines in its status log with the parameter's value substituted.
- **Other dialects:** each one's non-stopping message equivalent where it has one (e.g. Haas/Fanuc macro `#3006` stops, so not that one; a dialect with no non-stopping message says so in the post and is skipped).
- A probe op that sets no work offset (measure only) reports the same way, since then the message is the whole output.

**Done means:** the Tormach post emits one report line per probed axis, after the tolerance check and before `G10`, and a golden or test pins its text and position. Other dialects either emit their equivalent or are recorded as having none (decision file). A cutting op's output is unchanged.

Related: #362 / PR #521 (Tormach probing hooks), #522, #570, #574.

body:
Raised by the contributor during #521's hands-on probe test on a real Tormach 770MX, 2026-11-09 ("should we explicitly set S0? speed to 0 for probes").

**Today:** since #523 (PR #526) a probe op posts no spindle start (no `S0 M3`, no `M3`), and the program's only `M5` is at its end. The probe is safe on the 770MX because PathPilot's `M6` stops the spindle during the tool change. That is a property of the control, though, not something the program says. **Done means:** each shipped post (tormach, haas, fanuc, sinumerik, mazak, heidenhain) emits its spindle-stop word between the probe's tool change and its first motion. A test (alongside `probe_spindle`) pins the order per dialect, and a cutting op's output is unchanged.

title: Machine check refuses every probing program: a probe's rpm is judged against the spindle range

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
The machine limit check judges a touch probe's catalog `rpm` against the mounted machine's spindle range, so every probing program on a machine that states a minimum spindle speed is refused at post:

```
post blocked - machine Tormach 770MX: 1 limit problem(s): Probe X face: tool T99 Probe runs 1 rpm, below the machine's 175
```

Found while preparing the #521 hands-on probe test: catalog `PRB-0400` with the built-in Tormach 770MX (spindle 175-10000 rpm), Tormach PathPilot post.

**Cause:** `crates/app/src/machine/mod.rs` (~189-198) checks `tool.rpm` against `spindle_min`/`spindle_max` for every op, as the comment says ("today every op posts its tool's rpm"). A probe posts no speed at all: `posting.rs` forces rpm 0 for `ToolKind::Probe`, and #523/#526 posts no spindle start for it. So the probe's rpm field is never commanded, and judging it is a false refusal.

**Fix:** skip the spindle-range clause for probe tools (`ToolKind::Probe`), and for any op whose posted rpm is 0. Keep every other limit (axis travel, feeds) judged for probe moves.

Done means: a Probe op with the catalog probe posts on the Tormach 770MX (and any machine with a stated spindle minimum) with no limit problem, while a cutter below the minimum is still refused. Pinned by a machine-check test.

title: Locate the part in an imported fixture (or the fixture on the part) from the fixture and model pages

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Reported by the maintainer (filed by an agent), 2026-11-09: "we can import fixture. But we have no way of locating a part in the fixture on the fixture page or on the model page."

Part of #339 (fixtures/vises). Since #476/#549, a fixture's real mesh can be imported and is judged for collisions, but there's no way to put the part *in* it: the part and the fixture each sit where their files put them, so the collision verdict is only as good as that accidental placement.

**What's needed** (on the fixture page and the model page, the same tools both ways round):
1. **Mate by picks:** pick a face or point on the part, then the matching face or point on the fixture (a jaw face, a floor or parallel, a stop or locator pin). The part moves so the two coincide, with face normals opposed (part face sitting on the fixture face). Two or three mates fully locate it, the shop's 3-2-1 against a vise: the floor, the fixed jaw, then the stop.
2. **Numeric offset:** after a mate, nudge X/Y/Z (and a turn about the mate normal) by typed values. For example: 5 mm above the parallels, or 10 mm in from the stop.
3. **Move which one:** move the part into the fixture (default), or the fixture onto the part (common when the part is already aligned to the setup's plane, #330/#557, and the vise has to come to it).

**Rules:**
- **Commands:** every placement is one undoable command (`LocatePart` / `LocateFixture`), validated at creation and refused by name. That covers non-finite input, a degenerate pick (zero-area face, coincident points), a mate whose normals can't oppose, a placement that would leave the part interpenetrating the fixture (or at least warn by name), and no fixture or no model.
- **Frame:** the placement is relative to the setup the fixture belongs to. The setup's WCS (G54-G59, one per setup) is unchanged unless the user re-picks it. Stock follows the part as with part alignment (#326/#341).
- **Staleness:** moving the part or fixture marks that setup's ops stale (the collision verdict and toolpaths depend on it). Undo un-stales.
- **Shared code:** reuse the face/point pick from #554/#555/#557 so the setup and fixture tools share one picker, and the apply path from part alignment, so there's one transform model.

**Done means:**
- tests: a face mate sets the part's face coplanar with the fixture's, normals opposed; a 3-mate (floor, jaw, stop) gives a full location; a numeric offset moves the part exactly; LocateFixture moves the fixture, not the part; undo/redo walk each; degenerate picks are refused by name; the setup's ops go stale and the fixture collision check re-judges against the new placement.
- UI tests: the mate tools on the fixture page and the model page.

Related: #339, #476, #549 (fixture mesh and fixture UX), #330/#554/#555/#557 (alignment picks), #558 (WCS shown per setup).

title: Setup alignment: set the part's X and Y axis directions by picking an edge or two points

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Proposed by the maintainer (filed by an agent), 2026-11-09: picking the "Y" axis by either an edge or two points, and then X as well, should be an option for aligning parts to the WCS.

**What:** a setup alignment mode that orients the part *within* the work plane, after (or independently of) laying it flat:
- **Y axis:** pick a straight edge, or two points; their direction becomes the setup's +Y (the user can flip the sense).
- **X axis:** the same, by an edge or two points. When both are picked, X is projected so X and Y stay perpendicular (Y wins, or the user picks which is primary; record the choice). When only one is picked, the other follows from the work-plane normal (right-handed: X = Y × Z).
- The axes are measured in the work plane (projected onto it), so a slightly tilted edge still gives a clean in-plane direction. A direction too close to the plane normal is refused by name.

**Relation to the other alignment work:**
- #330 (reopened): face to plane sets the *plane* (which way is down). This sets the *in-plane rotation* (which way X/Y point), so together they give a full part frame.
- #554 drops edge picking for *plane* alignment on the setup page, because an edge can't define a plane. Edges are valid here, because an edge does define a direction. The setup page should make clear which pick each mode takes (face for plane; edge or two points for an axis), so the face pick no longer fights edge snapping.

title: Built-in VMC 3-axis blocks posting: Z stroke compared in the wrong coordinate frame
body:
The built-in **VMC 3-axis** machine (`assets/machines/vmc.mch`, mounted from the machine picker) states Z travel as `-500..0`. The posting limit check reads that stroke in **program coordinates through the active work offset** — so every move above the Z0 work origin is out of stroke: every retract, clearance and rapid gets reported, and posting is refused.

**Repro** (headless `camcraft-cli mcp`, current main `586092a8`): a 2D Contour on a 1 mm plate with normal clearance moves, document machine = built-in VMC 3-axis, `open_project` → `generate` → `verify`:

```
machine VMC 3-AXIS: 40 limit problem(s): 2D Contour1: move 0 reaches 26.000 in Z, the stroke is -500.000..0.000; ...
```

All 40 problems block the post. The program is clean: rapid at Z+26, approach at Z+3, cuts at Z 0..1 — physically well inside a 500 mm Z column on any real VMC.

**Why:** `-500..0` only makes sense in a machine frame zeroed at the top of the Z column. The checker converts moves to work-offset coordinates (`(w - origin[k]) * sign`, `crates/app/src/machine/mod.rs:337`) and compares them against the file's numbers directly; the module doc (lines 21-25) even states travel is read in program coordinates, but the `.mch` grammar offers no anchor tying a machine-frame stroke to a work offset. The #373 inverted-axis work handles sign only (`program_travel`, `crates/post/src/machine/direction.rs:87`) — the frame clash stands.

Notes:

- Each move is reported twice (both endpoints trip).
- X (±300) / Y (±250) follow the same convention: they pass only when the work origin happens to sit at table center.
- The default `3axis-vmc.mch` states no travel at all — an unstated limit checks nothing — so the same program passes on that def. Whether this check is signal or noise depends on which shipped def you mount. (Older saved projects whose embedded def lacks the Z travel line pass through for the same accidental reason; current builds round-trip the numbers faithfully.)

Fix directions, your call:

1. Restate the bundled def's numbers in the checker's documented convention — but a correct program-coords Z max is inherently work-offset-dependent, which the file cannot know.
2. Add a machine-frame anchor key to `.mch` that the checker converts through — #373's sign handling shows the seam already exists to extend.
3. Or drop `travel` from `vmc.mch` (like `3axis-vmc.mch`) so the default mount doesn't ship a check that contradicts its own convention.

title: Viewport: orthographic (parallel) projection option
body:
## What are you trying to do

I machine plates and brackets on my LinuxCNC machine, and most of my viewport time is setup work: looking straight at a side to line something up, judging an edge for parallelism, checking the part against the world axes, and reading the toolpath overlays. The view cube gives me the orientation (top/front/side is one click), but the projection stays perspective: edges converge, the silhouette drifts while I orbit or zoom, and a side view never looks "straight" the way a machinist's square looks straight. For CAM layout work I want a parallel (orthographic) projection most of the time.

This is the normal CAD/CAM convention - Fusion 360 defaults to a parallel projection with a perspective toggle next to it, and OnShape and SolidWorks do the same.

## How you imagine it working

- A Perspective / Orthographic radio pair beside the Shaded/Wireframe radios in the viewport panel. Default stays Perspective, so the current look never changes on open.
- A keyboard shortcut for the flip, in the same layer as the existing F/V/... keys.
- In ortho mode, the wheel scales the view height instead of the orbit distance; zoom-to-cursor stays cursor-anchored; and picking and every overlay (toolpaths, boundary viz, the view-cube HUD) read the same matrix the draw does, so nothing drifts.
- The view-cube face views become true ortho views in that mode. The mode rides as view state - a direct field flip like the display mode, never a command, never saved into the project.

Happy to build this - claim comment to follow.

title: Post gate refuses a clean 2D Contour: the column sim's inscribed arc chords clip a convex corner and read it as a 10 mm gouge

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
A 2D Contour around a plain L-shaped block generates with only the expected "Top below stock" rapid warning, but the post gate refuses it for a **10 mm gouge that isn't there**. The column engine of the program sim cuts each XY arc as chords drawn *inside* the arc (`arc_chords` at `chord_tol = cell / 4` = 0.094 mm). On a convex corner, the arc's centre is the part's own corner, so the simulated tool centre moves up to one sagitta closer to the part than the real G2/G3 does. One 0.375 mm column whose centre is 0.088 mm inside the corner gets clipped. Because the verdict judges each column by height alone, that clip counts as a gouge the full height of the wall.

Nothing unsafe reaches G-code: the gate *refuses* the post. But a correct program can't be posted, so this is a P1, not a P0.

### Part (our own geometry; rebuild it in any CAD)
In XZ, the profile is (-40,0) (40,0) (40,15) (10,15) (10,25) (-40,25), extruded from y -30 to 30. That gives a riser 25 mm high over x -40..10 and a lower step at z 15 over x 10..40. Export it as STEP.

### Reproduce (upstream/main 13802a1, `camcraft-cli mcp`)
1. `import_model {path: <part>.step, name: "StepBlock"}`
2. `set_stock {box: {dx: 90, dy: 70, dz: 28}}`, which puts the stock at x -45..45, y -35..35, z 0..28
3. `add_tool {catalog: "EM-0600-4FL"}`
4. `add_operation {kind: "2D Contour", tool: "EM-0600-4FL", name: "Contour1", source: "StepBlock"}` with default params: climb, side auto, stepdown 5, leave 0, top = top of model, bottom = bottom of model
5. `generate`, then `verify`

`verify` output:
- `rapid_in_stock`: "rapid move 1 travels below the clearance plane inside stock". This one is legitimate: top of model 25 is below stock top 28 and nothing faced it. It goes away with a Face op first, and the gouge stays.
- `post_gate`: **"gouge: program cuts below the model in 1 cell(s), worst 10.00 mm at (9.94, -29.94, z 15.00)"**

The same gouge shows with a Face op at stock top -3 ahead of the contour.

### Which moves
The contour walks the riser's section (x -40..10, offset by r = 3) at z 25, 20 and 15. Lower levels are skipped ("the part is solid below it"). Each level starts with the same corner arc around the riser's convex corner (10, -30):

```
  3 Feed (2.399,-33.902,25)->(10.346,-32.980,25)
  4 Feed (10.346,-32.980,25)->(13.000,-30.000,25) arc centre (10,-30)  <- R = 3 exactly
 19 / 34: the same arc at z 20 / z 15
```

Replaying the moves one at a time on the same `Dexel` (cell 0.375, x0 -45, y0 -35) lowers column (146,13), centre (9.9375, -29.9375), at **moves 4, 19 and 34 only**: 28 -> 25 -> 20 -> 15. The part's top at that centre is 25, which gives the 10 mm reading.

### Diagnosis: a verifier false positive from arc chord sagitta
- **The real path never touches that point.** The column centre is 0.088 mm from the corner, diagonally into the riser. The exact arc keeps the tool centre 3.000 mm from the corner, on the opposite side, so the nearest tool centre is about 3.06 mm away from the column centre. The cutter edge stays clear of it by about 0.06 mm. The generator-time verify finds no gouge.
- **The simulated path does touch it.** `Dexel::subtract` (crates/sim/src/stock_sim/dexel.rs) splits an XY arc with `cl::arc_chords(.., chord_tol)` and `chord_tol = dex.cell * 0.25` (cut.rs `simulate`). For this arc the first chord, (10.3457,-32.9800)->(11.6954,-32.4750), has a sagitta of about 0.086 mm, so its midpoint is 2.914 mm from the corner. Its distance to the column centre is **2.994 mm < r**. `cut_chord`'s exact reach test then lowers the column to z 25/20/15.
- **The height-only verdict blows it up.** `deviate` charges `sim - part` = 15 - 25 = -10, the full riser above the step. So a 6 µm overlap made up by the discretisation reads as a 10 mm gouge.
- Whether a column centre lands inside the sagitta band next to a convex corner depends on the lattice phase. That's why only this one corner of the four convex corners convicts.
- A related but separate effect: #299, a column a few µm inside a straight wall, judged by height alone. Fix 1 there (lateral slack in the verdict) would hide this case only if the slack is at least the chord sagitta. The cause here is in the sweep itself and is fixable on its own.

### Suggested fix (owner's call)
Make the column engine's swept disc never stand closer to the arc centre than the true arc does:
- Option A: cut XY arcs with an exact arc reach (distance from the column centre to the arc, the way `reach` is exact for segments).
- Option B: use circumscribed chords instead of inscribed ones (vertices pushed out by the sagitta) for the material-removal sweep.

Either way, a chord error must never push the simulated tool into the part. Check the bull/ball/cone kernels (`subtract_bull`, `subtract_ball`, `subtract_cone`) for the same issue.

**Done means:** this job (or a synthetic L-block in a box stock whose lattice puts a column centre within one sagitta of a convex corner) verifies with no gouge and posts. A test pins it. The existing gouge goldens still convict real gouges, including a deliberately undersized contour offset at a convex corner.

- **Body clearance.** From the tool body (#368 gives the import and placement), derive a minimum-radial-distance profile along Z.
- **Judging.** Judge that profile against the revolved in-process stock along each move, as a protected-move finding that blocks the post.
- **Fallback.** A turning tool without a body keeps today's behaviour, plus one named "holder not judged" note.

**Done means:** a modelled offset holder that rubs the shoulder of a stepped part is caught; the same move without a body is unchanged; goldens for one OD and one ID (boring bar) case.

Depends on the body import from #368.

title: Tool bodies from STEP: a vendor holder judged by its revolved envelope (milling)

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Part of #361 (vendor STEP tool models). First slice: milling.

**Today:** a tool's holder is one cylinder (`Tool::holder_d` / `holder_len`, `crates/tools/src/tools.rs`). Every mill check (shank/holder reach, multi-axis avoidance, fixture sweeps) judges stacked cylinders. A real holder or extension modelled by its maker can't be used.

**Proposed:**
- **Import.** Attach a STEP (or STL) body to a tool as its holder/assembly through the existing importer (`app/geometry/import/step.rs`), as one undoable command.
- **Placement.** The body is placed in the tool frame by numeric values: the axis it lies along, and the gauge/tip offset. No picking UI in this slice.
- **Envelope.** Derive its revolved envelope: the largest radius of the body in each band along the tool axis, conservative by construction. The existing cylinder-stack checks then judge that profile instead of the single holder cylinder. A tool without a body behaves exactly as today.
- **Persistence.** The body and its placement save and load in the project file (with a version rung if needed), and undo/redo walk it.
- **Refusals by name:** degenerate or non-finite bodies, an empty mesh, and a body that doesn't reach the tool axis.

**Done means:** a test holder STEP wider than its cylinder stand-in, at one height band, turns a move the cylinder passed into a named collision. A tool without a body is byte-identical to today. The project round-trips, undo restores the cylinder.

Not in this slice: the tool library file (see #348), viewport display, lathe holders, ISO 13399 coordinate systems.

title: Face and edge alignment trust facet winding - an inverted mesh lays the part upside down silently

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
From the independent re-review of PR #346 (#330), also true for the single-face pick and the 3-2-1 work-offset alignment (#187).

Face outward normals for alignment picks come from the facets' winding (`outward_normal`, used by `crates/app/src/pick/plane.rs` and `pick/align.rs`). Nothing checks the winding against the solid itself, so a model whose triangles are wound inside-out (a common STL export fault) gives inverted normals: "lay this face on G17" then turns the part upside down, and a 3-2-1 picks the opposite side, with no warning. Mis-orientation is gouge-class.

**Done means:** at import (or on first use), each closed body's winding is checked against its signed volume; an inside-out body is either repaired (all facets flipped, with a load note naming the body) or refused by name for alignment picks ("Face 12 belongs to a body whose facets are inside-out ..."); an open/non-manifold body whose outside can't be determined refuses face-normal picks by name. Pinned by tests with an inverted-winding cube for the plane pick, the two-edge pick and the 3-2-1.

Related: #330 (PR #346), #187, #326.

body:
**Proposal (for the owner to accept or decline):** a new user-facing command ships with an MCP tool, or with a filed follow-up issue.

**Why:** the MCP server (#128) lets an agent drive CamCraft headlessly: import, stock, tools, operations, generate, verify, post. **Possible rule text for AGENTS.md ("Everything Is a Command" section):**
> A PR that adds a user-facing command also adds its MCP tool (and script verb where it fits), or files a `source:agent` follow-up issue "MCP: <command>" and names it in the PR body.

**Possibly also:** a project skill, `.claude/skills/camcraft-mcp/`, describing the agent workflow and its known gaps:
- the workflow: open/import → set_stock → add_tool → add_operation → generate → verify → post;
- the param DTO shapes;
- refusals as data;
- the known gaps (machine and work offset not settable, no hole detection).

A contributor driving a job end to end over MCP (a simple plate on a Tormach 770MX, verified and run clean in PathPilot Hub) had to work these gaps out by hand.

title: Project load drops a stock's geometry revision, so save-load-save is not byte-identical after a stock edit

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
What happens: `model::set_facets` bumps an entity's geometry revision (`rev`) on every landing. The project loader pins `rev` back to the file's value for **models** (`project/apply.rs`, the `EntityKind::Model` arm, "the loader's pin is UNCONDITIONAL (M5.3 A)"), but the `EntityKind::Stock` arm calls `set_facets` and never pins. So a stock edited twice (e.g. `SetStock` twice) saves `"rev": 2`, loads as rev 1, and the re-save differs from the file it was opened from.

Expected: a stock's `rev` survives save/load like a model's (pin it after the stock arm's `set_facets`).

Evidence: found while working #326 - `AlignPartToSetup` re-meshed a box stock it had only moved and the round-trip test saw `"rev": 2` vs `"rev": 1` on the `Stock` entity. #326 now only re-meshes a stock whose size changed, which side-steps it; the loader gap itself is untouched. Staleness never reads `rev` (the stamp's signature does), so this is file-byte churn, not a wrong path.

Done means: save -> load -> save of a document whose stock was set twice is byte-identical, pinned by a project_roundtrip test.

title: A work offset rotation with non-finite values is treated as unrotated

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
From the independent review of PR #325 (#315, merged as be20197).

The new rotated-work-offset refusal (`crates/app/src/posting_wcs_rotation.rs`) measures the offset's total rotation angle and refuses anything above 1e-9 rad. A quaternion whose xyz parts are NaN or infinite falls through as "unrotated", so the offset would post as if it had no rotation. It is unchecked whether `SetWcsOrigin` (or the 3-2-1 align / project load paths) can ever store such a value; refusing it by name is the safe side either way.

Also noted: the setup sheet shows only the offset translation, so a rotation is invisible there.

**Done means:** a non-finite offset rotation (or origin) is refused by name at command creation (`SetWcsOrigin`, align, project load) and in the post check; the setup sheet states the offset's rotation when it has one; pinned by tests.

Related: #315, PR #325, #196.

title: Multi-pass, chamfer and taper turning passes rapid out through a longer bar

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Found by the independent review of PR #278 (which fixes the single profile/contour pass exit, #229).

#278 makes a turning pass that ends inside a longer bar leave its cut at feed: when the stock runs past the pass end, the exit is a feed at the plunge feed instead of a rapid through stock. But the **multi-pass, chamfer and taper** turning kinds still read no stock, so on a bar longer than the part they keep the old rapid exit - a G0 through material at the end of each pass.

Not yet reproduced with a test; whether the program sim or the rapid verdict catches it today is unchecked. If nothing refuses it, it is a silent rapid-through-stock (collision class) and should be raised to P0.

title: MCP: no way to detect holes for a Drill, Bore or Thread operation, so they always refuse
body:
The MCP server (#128) can add a Drill, Bore or Thread operation, but it can't fill the operation's hole list. Those kinds machine only the holes stored in their parameters, which the app fills from its **Detect holes** button. So over MCP a drill on a model with holes always refuses.

**Reproduced on `main` 8f30bee** (`camcraft-cli mcp`): `import_model` `testdata/models/Milling-test.step`, then `set_stock` `from_model`, `add_tool` `DR-0600`, `add_operation` `{kind: "drill", source: "part"}` and `generate`. The result is "Op: nothing to machine: no holes to drill". Bore with `EM-0300-2FL` gives "boring needs at least one hole".

**Root cause (confirmed):** the hole list is filled only by the UI's `State::detect_holes` (`crates/ui/src/state.rs`). It reads `operation::holes_of` (and `cross_holes_of` on a turret machine) and commits `EditOperationParams`. The MCP tool table (`crates/app/src/mcp/tools.rs`) has no tool that does this, and `edit_operation` would need the agent to compute hole coordinates itself.

**Fix:** move the rule out of the UI into `operation` (one function: the op's source, recognised, written into whichever hole list the kind has, plus the radial list on a turret machine, refusing by name otherwise). The UI's button and a new MCP tool `detect_holes {name}` both call it, so an agent's holes and a click's are the same, and the edit is one undo step. Pin: an MCP test detects the holes of a plate with a through hole, generates the drill, and `undo` empties the list again.

Related: #180 (MCP picks for faces, edges and loops) is the same gap for area operations.

title: Post gate refuses every 2D Chamfer and Deburr: the program sim judges the intended edge break as a gouge
body:
A 2D Chamfer or a Deburr generates with no warnings, but the post gate refuses it as a gouge. The program sim judges the edge break the operation exists to cut against the model's sharp edge. So no chamfer or deburr program can post whenever the sim judges it, which is any milled program in a box or model stock.

### Measured (main 8f30bee, scratch app test, the commands only)

Part: the 40 x 20 x 10 brick from `operations.rs`'s deburr test (`cube((-20,-10,0), (20,10,10))`). Stock: `FromModel` of the brick, a finished part, so nothing else is cut. Tool: `CM-0600-90`.

| Operation | Generator verify | Post gate |
|---|---|---|
| 2D Chamfer, kind defaults (width 0.8, 45 deg, side auto, top of model) | **0 warnings** | `gouge: program cuts below the model in 624 cell(s), worst 0.74 mm at (19.94, -9.81, z 9.26)` |
| Deburr, the suite's own params (width 2, window z 6..8) | 3 `RapidInStock` (a separate bug, filed separately) | `gouge: ... 1544 cell(s), worst 3.80 mm` |

For the Deburr I binned the gouge columns by depth: **1455 of the 1544 are 2 mm deep or less**. That's the 2 mm chamfer band itself; the 89 deeper ones are where its link rapid drags the cone. So even with clean links the deburr can't post.

### Why

- `stock_sim::simulate_document` judges the simulated stock against "the part as the machine must leave it": every model's facets, minus stock and fixtures (`stock_sim.rs`). `deviate_field` then charges every column cut more than `DEV_TOL` (0.01 mm) below the model as a gouge.
- The model has a sharp edge, and the chamfer and deburr ops cut a bevel into it by design. `operation/generate.rs` already says so for the leave-stock rule ("the chamfer cone owns its face outright", "the deburr cone owns its break outright"), but nothing tells the program sim.

### Possible fixes (owner's call: this is the gouge law)

1. **The ops own their break.** Before `deviate`, take each Chamfer2D or Deburr op's own swept cone (from its path and tool) away from the judged target, so their cut is "finished part" and anything else that cuts there is still judged. This keeps the gate strict everywhere else.
2. **A per-op allowance**: columns cut only by a chamfer or deburr op, within its stated width, are clean. That's simpler, but it needs per-column provenance in the sim.
3. If the intent is that a chamfer must be modelled in CAD first, the ops should refuse at generate ("the model has no chamfer here") instead of passing verify and failing at post.

A pinning test is the brick plus each op: it posts, and a deliberately deeper chamfer (width past the tool's reach, or a cone pushed into the wall) is still refused.

**Root cause (confirmed):** `simulate_document` judges against the model's facets only, and `deviate_field` charges every column cut more than 0.01 mm below them. Measured: 1455 of the deburr's 1544 gouge columns are 2 mm deep or less (its own break), and the 2D Chamfer gives 624 columns with a 0.74 mm worst and 0 generator warnings.

Suggested labels (I can't set them): `bug`, `P1`, `area:sim`, `area:2d`, `area:3d`, `source:agent`.

title: Post gate refuses a clean 2D Contour: the program sim reads a column 9 um inside a vertical wall as a full-height gouge
body:
A 2D Contour around the repo's own `testdata/models/Milling-test.step` generates with no warnings, but the post is refused for a 10 mm gouge that isn't there. The program sim reads a column whose centre is 9 µm inside a vertical wall as cut to the floor.

### Reproduce (main 8f30bee, `camcraft-cli mcp`, one line each)

```
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":0,"method":"initialize","params":{}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"import_model","arguments":{"name":"part","path":"testdata/models/Milling-test.step"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"set_stock","arguments":{"from_model":"part"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"add_tool","arguments":{"catalog":"EM-0600-4FL"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"add_operation","arguments":{"kind":"contour","tool":"EM-0600-4FL","source":"part","name":"Contour1","params":{"bottom_z":{"reference":"top_of_model","offset":-10}}}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":5,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"generate","arguments":{}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":6,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"verify","arguments":{}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"post","arguments":{"output":"contour.nc","post":"Fanuc"}}}
```

- `verify`: Contour1 has status ok and **0 warnings** (10 mm deep, inside the 15 mm flutes). The only finding is the gate's: `gouge: program cuts below the model in 1 cell(s), worst 10.00 mm at (22.32, 19.71, z 10.00)`.
- `post` is refused with the same line.

### What the toolpath actually does there

I checked it in a scratch app test: the same job built through the commands, every move's chords at 0.5 µm against the gouge column.

- The column's centre is (22.31802, 19.71006). The part's wall there is at y 19.71901 (the model's max Y), so the centre sits 9 µm inside the part.
- The nearest the tool centre ever comes to that point is **3.00895 mm** (move 368, a feed at z 15). With r = 3, the cutter edge stays **9 µm outside** the column centre. The path is exactly on the wall, as it should be.
- The sim (`stock_sim::simulate_document`, field arm, 0.375 mm cells) still reads that column's top at z 10, the contour's floor, so `deviate_field` reports `sim - part = 10 - 20 = -10`: a 10 mm gouge.

### Why

- `march_verdicts::deviate_field` (and the column engine's `deviate`) judge each column by height alone: the marched top at the column centre minus the part's top there. At a vertical wall, a column whose centre is a few µm inside the part flips from "full height" to "floor" on a sideways error far below the field's resolution. That error then reads as a gouge the depth of the wall.
- The viewer's eye doesn't do this. `preview::gate_tol(tol, cell)` judges a hit point by its distance to the model, with the march's landing slack (`HIT_GATE = 0.15` cells) added, and PR #288 reuses that for the machined mesh. So the post gate and the viewer can disagree about the same program.
- Whether a column centre lands in that sliver depends on the stock lattice's phase against the wall. I think that's why `lead_approach.rs`, which posts a contour on this same part in a box stock at z -7, doesn't hit it. I haven't checked that.
- A 3D Finish (BN-0600, kind defaults) on the same part with the same stock is refused with 37 gouge columns, the worst also at (22.32, 19.71) and the rest along the D's curved wall. That looks like the same mechanism, but I haven't measured those columns.

### Possible fixes (owner's call - the gouge law is the Prime Directive's)

1. Judge a gouge column against the **lowest part top within a lateral slack** of its centre (for example `gate_tol(DEV_TOL, cell)`), so a column within the field's resolution of a wall isn't charged the wall's height. It still convicts any cut that reaches past the slack.
2. Or judge the program gate the way the preview does: the distance from the marched surface point to the model, with the same gate. The gate and the viewer would then share one law.

Either way, a pinning test is this job (or a synthetic plate whose wall sits a few µm off a lattice centre), plus the existing gouge goldens to show real gouges still block.

**Also in a realistic setup** (main 8cf3c90, scratch app test): the same plate in `lead_approach.rs`'s own box stock (70 x 70 x 27 at z -7).
- A 3D Finish (`BN-0600`, kind defaults) is refused: `gouge: program cuts below the model in 37 cell(s), worst 22.01 mm at (-26.56, 13.94, z -2.01)`. Generator verify reports no gouge (only `ShankHit`).
- At that column I sampled every move at 0.01 mm. The ball reaches the column's centre line down to z -2.0103, the sim's own reading, with the line **0.00002 mm inside the ball**. The finishing ball is tangent to the wall, as it should be, and the column verdict charges the tangency as a 22 mm gouge.
- Boundary: in the same stock, a contour 10 mm deep is clean, which fits the verdict depending on where the lattice falls against the wall.

That narrows the cause. For the finish, the field reads the ball exactly, so the fault is the column verdict itself (`deviate_field` / `deviate`), not field interpolation. The contour case above (a cutter edge 9 um outside the centre, read as cut) still needs field slack on top of that.
**Root cause (confirmed):** `stock_sim::march_verdicts::deviate_field` charges a column by height alone, so a column centre 9 um inside the wall that the sim reads as cut becomes a 10 mm gouge. Measured: the cutter edge stays 9 um outside that centre, and the column reads z 10.

**Root cause (likely), not instrumented:** why the field reads that column as cut at all. My guess is the field's interpolation at 0.375 mm cells, but I didn't measure the march there.

Suggested labels (I can't set them): `bug`, `P1` (a clean program a user posts is refused), `area:sim`, `source:agent`.

title: A refused post's reason is only on the status line, and hover text erases it
body:
### What happens
A refused post (gouge, travel limits, a post-script warning such as #170's rigid-tap refusal on the Tormach 770M) writes no file, and the reason goes **only to the status line** (`crates/ui/src/state.rs` `post_program_path`: `self.status = format!("post refused: {err}")`). The status line is shared with hover text, so moving the mouse over the viewport replaces the reason at once ("no model under the cursor").

Found while testing PR #259 in the GUI: posting a tap job on the Tormach 770M produced no file and, as far as the user could see, **no message anywhere**. The refusal was there (pinned by `a_tap_job_posts_on_the_1100mx_and_is_refused_on_the_770m`), but it lived only for the instant before the next hover.

### Why it matters
Prime Directive: the output is either correct or **visibly** refused with a diagnostic. A refusal the user can't see looks like the Post button silently doing nothing.

### Suggested fix
Keep a post refusal on screen until the user dismisses it: a small modal or a sticky error banner with the full text (the gouge and limit lists can be long), and/or a refusal entry in the PostView pane. Hover text should never overwrite it. A UI test: a refused post leaves the reason visible after a hover update.

title: Take pixel snapshot goldens out of the PR flow; structural UI tests instead

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
## Problem

The UI suites compare rendered frames pixel-for-pixel against PNG goldens committed under `crates/ui/tests/snapshots/` (`egui_app.png`, `egui_app_light.png`, `egui_tool_editor.png`, ...). In the PR flow this costs more than it catches:

- **Every UI PR rewrites the same shared binaries.** PNGs can't merge, so any two open UI PRs conflict, and each merge re-conflicts the rest. On 2026-11-08, #201, #213, #232 and #234 each needed a maintainer refresh, and #213 and #232 needed it twice.
- **A regenerated golden proves little.** The fix for each conflict was to re-run with `UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1`, which accepts whatever the merged tree renders, so a real layout regression is accepted with it.
- **They're platform-sensitive.** A macOS run showed 1–4 px diffs on unchanged UI (the #234 review); the #201 review saw 5,328 scattered pixels. Real changes get lost in that noise.

## Proposal

1. **Take pixel snapshots out of the PR flow.** Mark the snapshot tests `#[ignore]` as a heavy-lane test named in the ignore reason, run at minor/major cuts via `scripts/gate.ps1 -Tier release`, and regenerated once at the cut in one commit. PRs never touch `crates/ui/tests/snapshots/*.png`.
2. **Replace them in the PR suite with structural UI tests.** egui_kittest exposes the AccessKit tree: assert that widgets exist, their labels and state, panel visibility, enabled/disabled cells, status-strip text. These are text-only assertions that diff and merge like code, are platform-independent, and fail with a readable message.
3. **Optional:** keep one pixel smoke test (the window renders non-blank) with a loose tolerance, in the same release lane.
4. **Process docs:** update AGENTS.md (Testing; drop the "regenerate goldens on merge" habit) and the gate maps, and say in the PR-review guidance that a PR must not change snapshot PNGs.

## Done means

- No test in the default/quick/batch tiers reads or writes `crates/ui/tests/snapshots/*.png`; the release tier runs them.
- Each existing pixel snapshot's intent is covered by at least one structural assertion.

title: Trochoidal toolpaths: constant-engagement loops for slots, channels and corners (Adaptive mode + standalone op)

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
## What

A **trochoidal toolpath strategy**: circular loops whose centre advances along the cut. It's the usual constant-engagement way to clear slots, narrow channels and corners, where a spiral or offset adaptive path would be forced into full-width (or a sudden jump in) radial engagement. Ship it as a selectable option for Adaptive clearing (2D and 3D levels), and as a standalone "Trochoidal slot" operation along a chain or centre line.

This is a feature request. The existing trochoid work (#5, #47, the M11.4 fallbacks) only covers Adaptive's *internal* fallback in slot-width channels and thin bands. This issue is the general, user-facing strategy.

## Background (public literature)

- **Geometry**, for a simple circular loop: x(φ) = B·cos φ, y(φ) = B·sin φ + S·φ/(2π), with B the loop radius and S the forward advance per revolution. For a slot of width W cut by a tool of diameter D, B = (W − D)/2. Epicycloidal and double-trochoid variants also exist.
- **Engagement angle** θ = θ_out − θ_in: the centre angle of the cutter's contact arc with the *current* stock, read at each point along the path.
- **Chip thickness** in the peripheral approximation is h(α) = f_z·sin α. On a trochoid the engagement window moves along the loop, so h varies; it isn't constant.
- **How constant engagement is kept:** evaluate θ against the live stock, and when it exceeds the limit, shrink the loop, cut the forward step, or reshape the loop, and/or drop the feed where θ rises.
- **References:**
  - Otkur & Lazoglu, "Trochoidal milling", IJMTM 2007: chip-thickness and force model, double trochoid.
  - Rauch, Duc & Hascoet, "Improving trochoidal tool paths generation and implementation using process constraints modelling", IJMTM 2009.
  - B-spline trochoid optimisation with a maximum-engagement constraint, Int J Adv Manuf Technol 2022 (doi 10.1007/s00170-022-09527-z).
  - Circular, trochoidal and epicycloidal parameterisations, Prod. Eng. 2021 (doi 10.1007/s11740-021-01060-4).

## Proposed parameters (user parameters with defaults)

- loop width (≤ the channel width − D, auto from the channel when unset)
- forward step per loop
- maximum engagement angle (or the equivalent optimal load)
- return arc: cutting / non-cutting with microlift (height) / retract
- feed on the cutting arc vs the return arc (the return arc at a higher "air" feed)
- direction: climb / conventional
- smoothing radius for the loop-to-loop transitions

## Done means

1. A trochoid generator in `crates/motion` that is engagement-controlled against the in-process stock: the loop and step adapt so θ ≤ the limit everywhere, and a refusal by name where the channel is narrower than the tool or the limit can't be met.
2. Adaptive gets a "trochoidal in slots/corners" mode that switches from the spiral to trochoidal loops where the spiral would exceed the limit (merges with, or replaces, #5's internal fallback).
3. A standalone Trochoidal slot operation along a picked chain or centre line, through `CreateOperation` / `EditOperationParams` with undo.
4. The verifier judges the loops: no gouge, the engagement limit holds (a measured θ trace in tests), and microlift returns land on air (#47).
5. Pins:
   - a full-width slot with θ_max under the limit, compared with a straight slot at 180°;
   - a corner that a spiral path overloads, cut within the limit;
   - a too-narrow channel refused by name;
   - post goldens on Fanuc, where arcs are written as G2/G3 when the post supports them.

Related: #5, #7, #44, #47 (Adaptive trochoid internals).

title: A fresh 2D Contour (any depth op) is refused when G54 Z sits on the part top: the default bottom is the G54 plane
body:
**What happens:** with G54's Z origin placed on the **top** of the part (a common habit, especially on Tormach mills, and what *Set origin* on a top face does), clicking **Milling 2D → 2D Contour** creates nothing. The status line says:

> operation not created: invalid parameters: a 2D Contour operation must cut downward: its top height resolves below its bottom height (check the From references)

The same applies to every depth kind seeded the same way (pocket, adaptive, offset…).

**Why:** a new operation's heights come from `Carried::of` (`crates/app/src/operation/kinds.rs`). Retyped from the default Face, which has no bottom, the fallback is:
- `top` = `TopOfModel + 0`
- `bottom` = `WorkOffset(0) + 0` (the G54 Z0 plane)

With G54 Z0 at the part top, bottom equals top, so the depth is zero. `CreateOperation` then refuses the operation before the user can open its Heights tab, and the only way through is to move G54 temporarily.

**Expected:** a fresh depth operation is created with a usable default whatever the work-offset convention, and the user then adjusts its heights.

**Proposed fix:** default `bottom` to `BottomOfModel + 0`. It meets the intent of `fresh_depth_operations_default_to_the_part_and_g54` (a fresh operation's numbers show where the material is) without depending on where G54 sits. That test pins the G54 default and would be updated.

**How it was found:** an outside contributor making a Face + 2D Contour job for a Tormach 770MX (#131), with G54 Z on the part top.

title: Lathe Facing faces the part model, not the stock allowance above it

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Found while fixing #89. The lathe Facing kind faces the part model, not the stock above it: with the part at its finished length it reports "nothing to face", so a bar's facing allowance declared in the setup stock cannot be faced off. Turning a bar to length - the first op on most lathe jobs - is therefore not expressible from stock, and drilling after facing (#89) can only be tested by modelling the allowance on the part.

Done means: Lathe Facing removes the stock above the part's end face (from the setup stock to the part's end), refusing by name when there is neither stock allowance nor part material to face; pinned by a bar with a 2 mm facing allowance in the stock that faces to the part end and lets a following axial drill post.

From #71. The robust axis fit sets small off-centre features aside, but it runs after the existing gate: if off-axis features make up more than ~10% of the surface (OK_SHARE 90%) or drag the plain fit past the 0.3 mm tolerance, the part is refused as not revolved before the robust pass sees it - e.g. a 20 mm keyway with a deep floor.
